name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Implement a real-time confidence scoring system for all AI-generated transcripts, enforced by the transcription team. This forces every output to meet the 65% minimum confidence floor before release, eliminating the risk of low-quality transcripts slipping through. The trade-off is slower turnaround for some videos, but that’s acceptable because bad transcripts damage trust more than delayed ones.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s confidence floor is a band-aid—it doesn’t fix the root: transcripts are already failing *before* scoring. The real risk is that we’re treating symptoms, not the broken ingestion pipeline that feeds garbage to the transcript team. Instead, task the ingestion team to add a 30-second pre-check for audio clarity and language match; if it fails, auto-reject and alert the source team. Settle it by running a 48-hour A/B test: measure transcript error rates with and without the pre-check, and kill the idea if it doesn’t cut errors by 40%.

name: Chisel
text:
Task the ingestion team to add a 30-second pre-check filter that rejects videos with audio clarity below 70% before they reach the transcript team. This stops garbage at the source, cutting downstream waste and speeding up the whole pipeline. The trade-off is a slight delay for some uploads, but it prevents far worse delays from failed transcripts.

name: Sift
text: The 30-second pre-check is a band-aid on a broken assumption: we’re measuring *audio clarity* when the real failure is *content suitability*. A 70% clarity score won’t stop a 10-second meme with perfect audio but no spoken words. Task the ingestion team to reject videos shorter than 30 seconds *or* with no speech detected—no scoring, just hard gates. Settle it with a 24-hour test: run the gate on 100 uploads and measure how many transcripts fail downstream.

name: Scope
text: Task the ingestion team to reject videos shorter than 30 seconds or with no spoken words before they reach the transcript team. This cuts the root cause—garbage in, garbage out—by stopping unsuitable content at the source. The trade-off is rejecting some short-form content, but it saves downstream time and avoids low-confidence transcripts entirely.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The 30-second cutoff is a blunt instrument—it will reject entire categories of legitimate short-form content like product demos or quick tutorials. Instead, task the ingestion team to flag videos shorter than 30 seconds for manual review by the curation team, who can decide suitability. Settle it with a two-week trial: measure how many valid short videos get rejected versus how many garbage ones slip through.

name: Reel
text: Task the ingestion team to add a real-time audio-to-text alignment check that flags videos where spoken words don’t match the expected duration. This catches mismatched audio/video, silent videos, and heavily edited clips before they hit transcription, cutting downstream waste by 40%. The trade-off is rejecting some borderline cases, but it’s the only way to stop the root cause without arbitrary cutoffs or manual reviews.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The audio-to-text alignment check assumes spoken words *should* match duration—it’ll fail on music videos, ASMR, or videos with heavy background noise where speech isn’t the primary audio. Task the ingestion team to instead flag videos with *zero* speech segments detected via a lightweight speech-vs-non-speech classifier; that catches silent or heavily edited clips without overfitting to duration. Settle it with a 1-week A/B test measuring downstream transcript failures.

name: Chisel
text: Task the ingestion team to reject videos with **zero speech segments detected** by a lightweight speech classifier before they reach the transcript team. This stops silent videos, music, or noise-only uploads at the source, cutting downstream waste by 30% without rejecting short-form content like demos or tutorials. The trade-off is missing some borderline cases where speech is faint but present, but the confidence floor of 65% ensures we don’t waste time on garbage.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s zero-speech filter will over-reject legitimate content like sign-language videos or narrated slides with background music—these fail the classifier but aren’t garbage. Task the ingestion team to route zero-speech videos to the curation team for a 30-second manual review instead; settle the argument by measuring how many of those rejections were false positives in a two-week pilot.

name: Scope
text: Task the ingestion team to reject videos with **zero speech segments detected** by a lightweight speech classifier before they reach the transcript team. This stops silent videos, music, or noise-only uploads at the source, cutting downstream waste by 30% without rejecting short-form content like demos or tutorials. The trade-off is over-rejecting sign-language videos or narrated slides with background music, but routing those to manual curation for a 30-second review keeps the filter precise.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Routing zero-speech videos to curation for 30-second review preserves sign-language and narrated slides but shifts waste from transcript to curation—30 seconds per video adds up to hours weekly. Task the curation team to build a 10-second triage rule: accept zero-speech if it’s a known sign-language channel or has on-screen text; reject otherwise. Settle when the rule is documented in the curation playbook and the team logs triage time weekly.

name: Reel
text: Task the ingestion team to reject videos with **zero speech segments detected** by a lightweight speech classifier before they reach the transcript team. This stops silent videos, music, or noise-only uploads at the source, cutting downstream waste by 30% without rejecting short-form content like demos. The trade-off is over-rejecting legitimate content like sign-language videos or narrated slides with background music—these will need manual review by curation.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: A 10-second triage rule for sign-language videos still risks misclassifying legitimate content—what if the classifier flags a 15-second ASMR video as "sign language" and sends it to curation? Instead, task the ingestion team to route *all* zero-speech videos to curation with a clear label: "No speech detected—verify if sign language or narrated slides." Settle it by measuring curation time per video and adjusting the threshold if waste exceeds 15 minutes daily.

name: Chisel
text: Task the ingestion team to route **all** zero-speech videos to curation with a clear label: "Needs Manual Review." This keeps sign-language and narrated slides out of the transcript pipeline while avoiding misclassification risks—curation’s 30-second review is the safest filter. The trade-off is shifting 30% of the workload from transcript to curation, but it prevents lost legitimate content and keeps the transcript team focused on high-value work.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s "Needs Manual Review" label shifts the bottleneck to curation—30 seconds per video *is* hours weekly, and their team isn’t scaled for that load. Instead, task the ingestion team to route *only* videos under 10 seconds with zero speech to curation; longer silent videos (sign language, narrated slides) get rejected outright. The artifact is a one-line rule in the ingestion classifier’s config, settled when the lead confirms the threshold change.

name: Scope
text: Task the ingestion team to route **all** zero-speech videos to curation with a clear label: "Needs Manual Review." This keeps sign-language, narrated slides, and rare edge cases out of the transcript pipeline while avoiding misclassification risks. The trade-off is shifting 30% of silent uploads to curation, but their 30-second triage is the safest filter—better than rejecting legitimate content or drowning the transcript team in noise.
